article_title: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://EdTrust.org
title: Professional development should build educators' culturally affirming skills, relationships, and anti-racist mindsets
description: The brief holds that to equitably support students' SEAD, educators must have the skills to create culturally affirming environments, build relationships with students, and support academic success, with mindsets geared toward anti-racism. It states that "Professional development (PD) ensures that educators learn these mindsets and skills," and urges states to support professional learning in asset-based pedagogies such as culturally responsive practices, diversity, equity, and inclusion, adult social-emotional learning or adult mindsets, and evidence-based, equity-focused systemic SEL for students. Washington already requires preparation programs to train teachers in culturally responsive pedagogy and provides online SEL modules for staff.
requirements: Preparation-program training requirements, licensure renewal tied to mastery of SEAD-supporting skills, and state agency staff to help districts identify and fund high-quality PD
constraints: Washington lacks clear equity-centered goals articulating a vision for PD addressing adult mindsets and SEL, and does not publicly report educators' perceptions of district PD offerings
target_learners: Educators in schools serving P-12 students
target_learning_goals: Culturally affirming environments, educator-student relationships, and support for students' academic success and well-being
examples: Washington requires preparation programs to provide training in effective, culturally responsive pedagogy and offers online SEL modules for staff
key_sources: How Does Washington Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. (2023). The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED630072

article_title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
citation: Feng, S., Koch, M. J., & Carolus, A. (2026). AI Mindset – An empirically tested theoretical framework on the psychological factors shaping AI competence and AI use. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100402
title: Professional development for teachers' AI engagement should extend beyond attitudes to develop pedagogical and ethical AI competence
description: Because pedagogical AI competence showed a strong positive association with AI use and carried several indirect associations from AI Mindset factors, the authors recommend that professional development address competence directly. The article states that "Professional development programmes should therefore extend beyond attitudes towards AI to include the development of AI competence, particularly pedagogical and ethical competences." This follows from the finding that openness, relatedness and effort appraisals related to AI use indirectly through competence.
requirements: Programmes must address pedagogical and ethical AI competence, not only attitudes towards AI
constraints: Based on cross-sectional associations among teachers predominantly recruited from the KI@School project; causal direction not established
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical and ethical competence in using AI in teaching practice
examples: The study's SEM showed pedagogical AI competence significantly associated with AI use (β = 0.45, p < .001) and mediating several AI Mindset factor associations
key_sources: Feng, S., Koch, M. J., & Carolus, A. (2026). AI Mindset – An empirically tested theoretical framework on the psychological factors shaping AI competence and AI use. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100402

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: PD design pattern pairing new activities with specific facilitation moves to support equity-oriented sensemaking
description: In the redesigned Summer 2 PD, each new activity was deliberately paired with a facilitation conversation targeting a specific ideological challenge: "Language Storybook was paired with a conversation about recognizing multilingual learners' assets; Jonathan and the Sun was paired with a conversation about surfacing deficit ideologies grounded in teachers' experiences" (Design section). This pairing links immersive experiences of being a nondominant-language learner to explicit discussion of ideologies, giving facilitators structured openings to surface and challenge deficit framings rather than pivoting back to safer content-focused ground.
requirements: Activities must be paired with conversations that connect the immersive experience to teachers' own planning, teaching, and ideological assumptions
constraints: The facilitation moves examined concern multilingual learners' assets and deficit ideologies in K-4 elementary science PD
target_learning_goals: Ideological sensemaking and rearticulation toward equity-as-transformation perspectives
examples: Summer 2 designers paired the French storybook debrief with asset recognition talk and the Jonathan and the Sun reading with surfacing deficit ideologies from teachers' experiences
key_sources: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Situate teachers' professional development in the kinds of learning environments and communities they are encouraged to create for their students
description: From the USA case, the article proposes that professional development should "allow teachers to work and learn within the kinds of learning environments and professional learning communities they are encouraged to create for their students, and provide support throughout the implementation process." The idea is that teachers experience participatory learning first-hand during PD, so they can later foster the same participatory environment for their students; the Case 1 workshop was structured accordingly, with teachers first learning a core participatory instructional routine before designing it into their online courses.
requirements: Support throughout the implementation process; curricular designs should foster connected learning and productive disciplinary engagement while supporting conventional literacies and academic knowledge for which teachers are accountable.
constraints: The article's principle list also states the approach must "accommodate prevailing levels of student network access" and "make reasonable demands on teachers' time for designing and delivering curricula."
target_learning_goals: enacting participatory and personalized learning approaches
designing technology-enhanced curricula
examples: The workshop initiated with teacher learning activities around the core participatory instructional routine, which was effective in helping teachers appreciate the central role of learner agency in participatory teaching.
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7

article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: Five-month workplace-based PD program blueprint for teacher differentiation skills
description: A professional development program designed with 4C/ID and the Ten Steps to teach primary school teachers differentiated instruction in mathematics. It combines three initial group meetings (interactive lectures, modeling examples, imitation tasks), four four-week task classes of daily classroom practice with individual coaching based on classroom recordings, cognitive feedback against 30 performance standards, and team reflection sessions. The article states "it resulted in a detailed blueprint of a five-month professional development program that strategically combines learning activities to stimulate learning processes that are essential for developing the complex skill providing differentiated instruction in a mathematics lesson."
requirements: Participating schools must show that at least 80% of the teacher corps is willing to participate voluntarily; teachers should possess at least a basic level of teaching and classroom management skills
constraints: Classroom management training was outside the program's scope; part-task practice was not included because no skills required automation
target_learners: in-service primary school teachers in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: providing differentiated instruction in mathematics lessons
examples: Group meeting 1 built a shared mental model of DI and addressed misconceptions; task classes followed an identical organization with lecture, coaching, and reflection
key_sources: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x

article_title: Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review
citation: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z
title: Taxonomy of PDW payoff schemes: four-cell matrices versus free-choice designs
description: The review organizes the heterogeneous payoff systems used in post-decision wagering into two broad classes: four-cell matrices, where a low and a high wager option combine with correct and incorrect responses to yield four possible outcomes, and free-choice designs with more than four cells. It reports that "A total of 78 four cell matrices (70% of all reviewed payoff schemes) were retrieved from the literature" and that "In total, 33 such free choice designs were retrieved from the literature (30% of all reviewed payoff schemes)". Within these classes it further distinguishes no-wager/safe-option variants, always-wager-high matrices, no-loss gambling, adjusted wagering, and designs matching other instruments.
requirements: A payoff scheme must be fully described in terms of wins and losses following wagers after correct and incorrect decisions to be classifiable
constraints: The review covers only original empirical studies using PDW published in English-language journals, identified via Web of Science and APA PsycNet searches in June and July of 2023
target_learners: researchers designing or evaluating metacognition studies using post-decision wagering
target_learning_goals: assessing confidence and metacognitive awareness with appropriately designed payoff schemes
key_sources: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z

article_title: Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review
citation: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z
title: Design PDW payoff schemes in light of the specific research question; there is no single best practice
description: The review concludes that payoff design choices in post-decision wagering cannot follow one universal recipe: "it is clearly not the case that there is a single 'best practice' PDW procedure. Rather, the issues outlined here need to be considered in light of a specific research endeavor in order to determine the best design choices for the question at hand." Designers should weigh restriction of wager choice, safe or no-wager options, optimal-strategy analysis, loss aversion, and confidence-adjusted payoffs against their research goals.
requirements: Designers must consider the issues outlined (wager restriction, safe options, optimal strategies, loss aversion) in light of their specific research endeavor
constraints: Some difficulties can be circumvented via careful payoff design, but other issues, such as why participants deviate from optimal strategies, remain open questions
target_learners: researchers designing or evaluating PDW payoff systems
target_learning_goals: selecting payoff schemes that yield interpretable confidence or awareness measures
examples: The review documents that none of the reviewed payoff matrices follow the Schurger & Sher proposal of a low option punishing at chance via small wins and losses and a high option not punishing at chance but with large wins and losses
key_sources: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Four guiding principles for fostering productive disciplinary engagement
description: Engle and Conant proposed four guiding principles for fostering productive disciplinary engagement: "(1) problematizing content from each student's own viewpoint, (2) giving students authority to address these problems, (3) holding students accountable to each other and disciplinary norms, and (4) providing appropriate resources for accomplishing the first three." The article reports these have become among the most influential instructional strategies to emerge from situative perspectives, and that studies embodying the principles most strongly showed the strongest PDE outcomes.
requirements: All four principles must operate together; authority must be balanced with accountability
constraints: Too much authority and too little accountability leads students away from participation in the discipline
target_learning_goals: Productive, disciplinary, and sustained engagement with content
examples: Engle's 2012 retrospective review of 23 PDE studies rated each study's embodiment of the four principles and associated outcomes
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Does Professional Development Effectively Support the Implementation of Inclusive Education? A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johanna L. Donath, Timo Lüke, Elisabeth Graf, Ulrich S. Tran, Thomas Götz. (2023). Does Professional Development Effectively Support the Implementation of Inclusive Education? A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09752-2
title: Design inclusive-education professional development with active learning, practical relevance, and participation prerequisites to facilitate transfer to schools
description: The meta-analysis examined the Desimone design criteria (content focus, coherence, active learning, collective participation, duration) plus certification for professional development addressing inclusive education. It found that "long-term training with high practical relevance and active learning opportunities facilitates transfer to schools", though support for the classic criteria was limited overall. Active learning significantly moderated skill gains, and participation prerequisites and specific content focus improved some subcategory outcomes.
requirements: Programs should provide practice opportunities within sessions, case studies, and alternating input and praxis phases rather than blocked input-only sessions.
Participation prerequisites (e.g., having a relevant student in the classroom) and coherent additional learning activities support transfer.
constraints: Descriptions of program design in primary studies were scarce, so design effects may be underestimated.
Moderator analyses were limited to intensive intervention programs; data from short-term one-shot programs were lacking.
Duration showed no influence when analyses were limited to programs up to 200 h.
target_learning_goals: knowledge about inclusive education
inclusive teaching skills
positive beliefs toward inclusive education
improved student behavior
examples: Programs with alternating input and praxis phases showed larger changes in use of teaching methods (g = 0.78) than blocked-design programs (g = 0.03).

Programs requiring teachers to fulfill participation prerequisites reported larger changes in perception of teaching methods (g = 0.60) and student achievement (g = 0.71) than programs open to all teachers.
key_sources: Johanna L. Donath, Timo Lüke, Elisabeth Graf, Ulrich S. Tran, Thomas Götz. (2023). Does Professional Development Effectively Support the Implementation of Inclusive Education? A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09752-2

article_title: Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement
citation: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8
title: Use rapid PDSA cycles to test and adapt AIEd systems to local contexts
description: The article advocates Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles as disciplined inquiry routines for testing a working theory of adapting an AIEd system to local context. It argues PDSA cycles "encourage stakeholders to address failure, negative outcomes, and unintended consequences quickly and intentionally" and develop teachers' ownership by "alleviating the potential impact and fear of getting it wrong." As redesign cycles unfold, understanding of the AIEd system evolves toward more robust tools.
requirements: Prediction as part of disciplined inquiry, "like all experimental learning"
Collaborative structures and guidance for researchers and practitioners
constraints: Small rapid tests are framed as learning routines, not as large-scale efficacy trials
target_learners: Teachers, researchers, and developers co-improving AIEd tools
target_learning_goals: Learning quickly from failures and successes when adapting AIEd systems
examples: Practitioners would deploy rapid tests of change to guide the development, revision and continued fine-tuning of a tool instead of abandoning it when results disappoint
key_sources: Bhimdiwala, A., Neri, R. C., & Gomez, L. M. (2022). Advancing the Design and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Education through Continuous Improvement. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00278-8

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement
citation: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302
title: Logic model linking PD interventions to teacher knowledge, classroom instruction, and student outcomes
description: Adapted from Garrett et al. (2019), this model structures the meta-analysis: "teachers' participation in a PD may lead to changes in their knowledge (Path a) and/or changes in classroom instruction (Path b); changes in instruction may also operate through changes in knowledge (Path f)." Changes in teachers then affect student outcomes (Paths h and i), while interventions may also affect students directly through new materials and supports (Path c), with context and intervention characteristics as moderators (Paths d, e, and g). The present analyses test Paths a, b, d, e, h, and i.
requirements: Empirical tests require studies measuring both teacher-level outcomes (knowledge and/or instruction) and student achievement outcomes within the same randomized contrast
constraints: Prior meta-analyses primarily analyzed Paths b and i; Paths a and h were examined only via intervention-impact associations, not within-study correlations
target_learning_goals: mathematics and science achievement
teacher knowledge
classroom instruction
examples: The study examines Paths a and h — PD impacts on teacher knowledge and their link to student learning — which prior meta-analyses had not analyzed
key_sources: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302

article_title: Power Analysis for Cross Level Mediation in CRTs
citation: Ben Kelcey. (2014). Power Analysis for Cross Level Mediation in CRTs. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract.
title: Applied power-analysis of 3-2-1 mediation designs using design parameters from a large professional development study
description: The article reports an application of its framework using "data from a large study of many different professional development programs" to design studies examining "the extent to which teachers' knowledge mediates the relationship between participation in a professional development program and students' cognitive development". The application examines designs that achieve 80% power based on design parameters such as ICC and effect size drawn from this study and other studies. It serves as a worked instantiation of the power framework for planning multilevel mediation studies in education.
requirements: Empirical estimates of design parameters (e.g., intraclass correlations, effect sizes) from the professional development study and other studies, as the article states these parameter values are used to identify designs achieving 80% power
constraints: Results were not presented due to space constraints, so the specific parameter values and resulting design sizes are not printed in this abstract
target_learners: education researchers planning professional development efficacy studies
target_learning_goals: designing studies powered to detect mediation of professional development effects through teacher knowledge
examples: The application examines designs achieving 80% power for detecting whether teachers' knowledge mediates the relationship between professional development participation and students' cognitive development
key_sources: Ben Kelcey. (2014). Power Analysis for Cross Level Mediation in CRTs. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562757

article_title: Focusing on Teacher-Student Interactions Eliminates the Negative Impact of Students' Disruptive Behavior on Teacher Perceptions
citation: Hafen, C. A., Ruzek, E. A., Gregory, A., Allen, J. P., & Mikami, A. Y. (2015). Focusing on teacher–student interactions eliminates the negative impact of students’ disruptive behavior on teacher perceptions. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025415579455
title: Professional development focused on developmentally sensitive teacher–student interactions can alter teachers' internal views of students
description: The article argues that interventions targeting classroom interactions can change how teachers perceive students, not just their behavior: "the view teachers have of their students is malleable and a focus on increasing developmentally sensitive interactions in the classroom through a relatively low-cost intervention can be impactful." MTP-S coaches teachers to place student behavior in developmental context and treat students in individualized ways.
requirements: Coaching grounded in a framework of high-quality teacher–student interactions (CLASS-S) with sustained support across the academic year
constraints: Evidence comes from one academic year in five mid-Atlantic US schools; the authors call for future implementations in different contexts
target_learning_goals: teacher perceptions and expectations for students
developmentally sensitive teaching interactions
examples: MTP-S teachers in the trial showed no significant link between student disruptive behavior and lower projections, unlike control teachers
key_sources: Hafen, C. A., Ruzek, E. A., Gregory, A., Allen, J. P., & Mikami, A. Y. (2015). Focusing on teacher–student interactions eliminates the negative impact of students’ disruptive behavior on teacher perceptions. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025415579455

article_title: Professional Development in Classroom Assessment: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Sanusi, N., Zulkifli, H., Hamzah, M. I., & Jait, K. (2025). Professional development in classroom assessment: a systematic literature review. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn). https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v19i4.22026
title: Four-theme taxonomy organizing professional development in classroom assessment research
description: The review organizes 43 studies into four themes: assessment in education, classroom practices and teacher development, student-centered education, and specialized education and teacher training. This taxonomy maps the field's coverage and identifies where research effort is concentrated. The article states: "The categorization of all publications was based on four primary themes: assessment in education (8 articles), student-centered education (3 articles), classroom practices and teacher development (10 articles), and specialized education and teachers (21 articles)."
requirements: A corpus of empirical studies on professional development in classroom assessment retrieved through structured database searches
constraints: Limited to journal articles published 2021-2023 in English from Scopus and Web of Science
target_learning_goals: Understanding the landscape of professional development in classroom assessment research
key_sources: Sanusi, N., Zulkifli, H., Hamzah, M. I., & Jait, K. (2025). Professional development in classroom assessment: a systematic literature review. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn). https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v19i4.22026

article_title: Application of the PDCA cycle management in quality improvement of endotracheal intubation in emergency department among standardised training residents.
citation: Tan Zhanpeng, Lai Fang, Li Xiaoya, Li Deyang, Li Hui, Liu Shiyi, Yang Suyi, Yan Chunjiang, Li Guowei, He Fengxian, Zeng Ruifeng, Li Huanmei. (2026). Application of the PDCA cycle management in quality improvement of endotracheal intubation in emergency department among standardised training residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09076-z
title: PDCA cycle management as a four-phase continuous quality improvement framework for procedural training
description: The PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle, "also known as the 'quality loop', is a management approach for continuous improvement". In this article it organizes ETI training for standardised training residents: Plan sets goals and key indicators, Do implements tiered training, SOPs and quality control, Check monitors real-time procedural compliance and feeds back data weekly, and Act implements targeted optimisations such as mandatory airway assessment. Root-cause analysis via a fishbone diagram identified factors in four aspects: "man, material, method and environment".
requirements: A PDCA team conducting root cause analysis and demonstration of possible influencing factors
Real-time monitoring documentation and weekly data feedback meetings
constraints: Applied in a single emergency department with standardised training residents; the authors note it is a single-center retrospective study subject to temporal confounding
target_learners: standardised training residents rotating through the emergency department
target_learning_goals: endotracheal intubation technique
difficult airway identification and management
complication prevention
key_sources: Tan Zhanpeng, Lai Fang, Li Xiaoya, Li Deyang, Li Hui, Liu Shiyi, Yang Suyi, Yan Chunjiang, Li Guowei, He Fengxian, Zeng Ruifeng, Li Huanmei. (2026). Application of the PDCA cycle management in quality improvement of endotracheal intubation in emergency department among standardised training residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09076-z
